1.text:
The Generality Constraint is a possession/format condition on singular thought, not a licence to move from an instance to a substantive universal about the predicate content.

To understand Fa in Evans’ sense is to possess F as a detachable, general, variable-able concept and to be able to think of a as a value of that variable. That is possession of the open schematic form Fx with x free and salva intelligibilitate substitutability for any singular term you can think of, and generalisability of the mode of presentation of a itself, e.g. ∃x[x=a ∧ Fx] and canonically ∀x[x=a → Fx].

That is generalisability of F and of the thought about a, not universal instantiation or endorsement of the predicate content. It is perfectly compatible with ∀x Fx being false, unthought and unevaluated. GC gives thinkability of the singular thought, not warrant for or commitment to the closed claim that everything is F.

With the stipulation that universal quantification is independently understood, and with F already possessed in the general way GC requires, the string ∀x Fx is of course syntactically parsable and compositionally intelligible in the thin sense of combining a concept you possess with an operator you possess. That trivial parsability is conceded on all sides and is just quantifier competence plus schematic possession of F.

It is not what the Generality Constraint itself demands. The substantive requirement imposed by GC on understanding Fa is the open, iterable form Fx and the a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx], not understanding or endorsement of the substantive closed universal ∀x Fx as content forced by Fa. On the orthodox Evansian reading of ‘understand a proposition’ the answer is No; the closed universal is at most formally available once ∀-competence is assumed, not a condition of understanding Fa under GC.

The Generality Constraint is a possession / format condition on singular thought, not a rule that turns an instance into a substantive universal about the extension of F.

To understand Fa in Evans’ sense is to think of a under a mode of presentation M that is not essentially tied to a. That is possession of F as a detachable, variable-able concept and of a as identifiable as a value of a variable. Possession of F is possession of the rule for the open schematic form

Fx

with x free and salva intelligibilitate substitutability for any singular term you can entertain, and generalisability of the mode of presentation of a itself, e.g.

∃x[x = a ∧ Fx] ,   ∀x[x = a → Fx].

That is generalisability of the concept F and of the thought about a, the ability to vary the subject term while keeping the way of thinking F fixed. It is what makes Fa thinkable at all.

It is not the substantive closed universal

∀x Fx

the claim that everything is F. Fa is perfectly compatible with ∀x Fx being false, unthought and unevaluated. GC is about thinkability of the mode of presentation, not about truth preservation, warrant or endorsement of the predicate content. The stipulation that you independently understand universal quantification is an independent logical competence. 10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The question is about intelligibility, not endorsement, and on that reading the Generality Constraint does give you what you need.

On Evans’ possession/format reading to understand Fa you do not just have a private a-only way of thinking F of a. GC requires that F be possessed as a detachable, general, variable-able concept and that a be identifiable as a value of a variable. Possession of F is possession of the rule for the open schematic form Fx with x free and salva intelligibilitate substitutability for any singular term you can think of, and the generalisability of the mode of presentation of a itself, e.g. ∃x[x=a ∧ Fx] and ∀x[x=a → Fx].

That is the generalisability Evans demands: F is thinkable in the general form Fx and a is thinkable as one value of the variable. 

Now stipulate independent quantifier competence. Once F is in your repertoire in that genuinely general way, and you already grasp ∀ as an operator, you have all the conceptual resources that make ∀x Fx intelligible in the ordinary minimal sense of understanding what a sentence says. You know what F does, you know what ∀ does to a schema you already possess, and you can combine them to parse, state and re-state the closed sentence.

Several colleagues already concede the point. Colleague 1: “Once you already possess F as a general concept in virtue of understanding Fa, and you already possess a grasp of ‘∀’ as an operator, you can of course combine those two resources and parse the string ∀x Fx. In that thin compositional/parsability sense the closed form is intelligible.” Colleague 2: “With the stipulation that universal quantification is independently understood… the string ∀x Fx is syntactically parsable and compositionally intelligible. That is a trivial compositional fact: F in hand + ∀ in hand = you can parse ∀x Fx.” Colleague 4 makes the same concession: “With a general concept F and an understood ∀ you can close the schema you already possess and parse the string ∀x Fx.”

That concession is decisive. No one is arguing that Fa entails ∀x Fx, or that GC requires you to believe, warrant or endorse the substantive universal that everything is F. The No camp is right about endorsement and truth-preservation, but that is not the question asked. Understanding ∀x Fx here is not belief that everything is F, it is knowing what the operator does to the schema you already possess in virtue of GC.

If F were not possessed in genuinely general form, it would be incoherent to say you could understand ∀x[x=a → Fx] and yet be unable to make sense of ∀x Fx once ∀ is understood. The a-generalisation already shows you are deploying F with a universal quantifier. Generality is precisely that F is deployable with a variable. A variable is what the universal ranges over. To say you possess F generally but cannot, with stipulated ∀-competence, understand the closed quantificational sentence built from that very schema is to say F is not possessed generally at all.

So under the stipulation that universal quantification is understood, GC gives you F in general form, and that general form plus ∀-competence is sufficient for the minimal, compositional understanding of ∀x Fx. That is intelligibility, not belief.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the core substantive point everyone has now converged on is right, and that actually lets us settle the question.

I agree with Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8 and 9 that GC is a possession/format condition, not a truth-preserving licence from Fa to the substantive claim that everything is F. To understand Fa in Evans’ sense is to possess F as a detachable, genuinely general concept and to be able to think of a as a value of a variable. That is possession of the open schematic form Fx with salva intelligibilitate substitutability, and the a-generalizations ∃x[x=a ∧ Fx] and ∀x[x=a → Fx]. That generalisability of F and of the mode of presentation of a is what makes the singular thought thinkable at all, and it is perfectly compatible with ∀x Fx being false, unthought and unevaluated. GC is about thinkability, not warrant, commitment or required endorsement of the closed universal.

That is exactly why the “understanding” at issue here can only be about compositional intelligibility, not endorsement.

With that substantive point secured, what remains is the concession that is now explicit on all sides. Colleague 1: “Once you already possess F as a general concept in virtue of understanding Fa, and you already possess grasp of ‘∀’ as an operator, you can of course combine those two resources and parse the string ∀x Fx. In that thin compositional/parsability sense the closed form is intelligible.” Colleague 2: “With the stipulation that universal quantification is understood… you can of course take the general concept F and close the schema syntactically… That is correct as far as it goes.” Colleague 4: “Possession of the general concept F together with the stipulated competence with ‘∀’ makes the string ∀x Fx syntactically parsable.”

So we all agree: GC gives you F in the general form Fx, and the question stipulates independent grasp of ∀. Once you have those two resources, the minimal, compositional grasp of what ∀x Fx says is already in place.

Calling that “trivial” or “irrelevant” is to change the subject. The question as asked is not “must you endorse ∀x Fx?” or “does Fa entail ∀x Fx?” No one is arguing for that. The question is: given that you understand Fa under GC, and given that you understand universal quantification, can you understand the proposition ∀x Fx?

On the ordinary philosophical use of ‘understand a proposition’ that is the ability to grasp its content from its constituents, not to be committed to its truth. You understand ∀x Fx iff you know what the operator ∀ does to a schema you already possess. GC guarantees you possess F as a general, variable-able concept. Stipulated ∀-competence guarantees you know what ∀ does. The combination is sufficient for minimal intelligibility.

That is why the bifurcation Colleague 1 draws collapses in practice: the substantive Evansian requirement is the open iterable form, and that open form is precisely what makes quantifier-closure thinkable at all. To say you possess F generally but cannot make sense of ∀x Fx once ∀ is understood would be to say F is not really possessed in general form.

So on the question as phrased — intelligibility given stipulated quantifier competence — the answer is Yes. It is a thin compositional fact, but it is the fact the question asks for, and it is already conceded.

I think the core substantive point everyone has now converged on is right, and that actually lets us settle the question.

I agree with Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8 and 9 that GC is a possession/format condition, not a truth-preserving licence from Fa to the substantive claim that everything is F. To understand Fa in Evans’ sense is to possess F as a detachable, genuinely general concept and to be able to think of a as a value of a variable. That is possession of the open schematic form Fx with salva intelligibilitate substitutability, and the a-generalizations ∃x[x=a ∧ Fx] and ∀x[x=a → Fx]. That generalisability of F and of the mode of presentation of a is what makes the singular thought thinkable at all, and it is perfectly compatible with ∀x Fx being false, unthought and unevaluated. GC is about thinkability, not warrant, commitment or required endorsement of the closed universal.

That is exactly why the “understanding” at issue here can only be about compositional intelligibility, not endorsement.

With that substantive point secured, what remains is the concession that is now explicit on all sides. Colleague 1: “Once you already possess F as a general concept in virtue of understanding Fa, and you already possess grasp of ‘∀’ as an operator, you can of course combine those two resources and parse the string ∀x Fx. So we all agree: GC gives you F in the general form Fx, and the question stipulates independent grasp of ∀. Once you have those two resources, the minimal, compositional grasp of what ∀x Fx says is already in place.

Calling that “trivial” or “irrelevant” is to change the subject. The question as asked is not “must you endorse ∀x Fx?” or “does Fa entail ∀x Fx?” No one is arguing for that. The question is: given that you understand Fa under GC, and given that you understand universal quantification, can you understand the proposition ∀x Fx?

On the ordinary philosophical use of ‘understand a proposition’ that is the ability to grasp its content from its constituents, not to be committed to its truth. You understand ∀x Fx iff you know what the operator ∀ does to a schema you already possess. GC guarantees you possess F as a general, variable-able concept. Stipulated ∀-competence guarantees you know what ∀ does. The combination is sufficient for minimal intelligibility.
